records.name: Agnelli–Elkann family (Fiat, Exor)
records.scaleNote: Exor, the family's listed holding, reported a net asset value of €33.2bn and gross assets of €37.1bn at 31 December 2025, and is the largest shareholder of Ferrari, Stellantis, Philips and CNH.
records.origins: Giovanni Agnelli (1866–1945), a cavalry officer from a Piedmontese landowning family, was among the founding investors of Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino (FIAT) in Turin in 1899 and soon became its dominant shareholder. His grandson Gianni Agnelli (1921–2003) chaired Fiat from 1966 to 1996.
records.role_summary: The fortune was made by building Fiat into Italy's dominant carmaker and industrial group in the 20th century, then holding it through a chain of family holding companies (IFI, IFIL, now Exor). From 2009 the Fiat group was split and recombined: Chrysler (2014), the Ferrari spin-off (2016), CNH and Iveco, and the 2021 Fiat Chrysler–PSA merger that created Stellantis. Exor, controlled by the family partnership Giovanni Agnelli B.V., keeps the largest stakes in each.

roleDetail.d: Giovanni Agnelli joined the group of Turin investors that founded FIAT in 1899 and took control of the company in its first decades.
Under Gianni Agnelli Fiat became Italy's largest private industrial group, with interests across cars, trucks, newspapers (La Stampa) and Juventus football club.

After the deaths of Gianni (2003) and Umberto Agnelli (2004), John Elkann, Gianni's grandson, took over the family's leadership; Sergio Marchionne's Fiat merged with Chrysler, then spun off Ferrari (2016) and the industrial arm CNH.
Exor merged its Italian parent into a Dutch N.V. in 2016 and is listed in Amsterdam; the Netherlands allows loyalty (special voting) shares that give long-term holders extra votes.
Exor sold about 4% of Ferrari in 2025 for about €3bn and keeps about 20% of Ferrari's economic rights and 30% of its votes, while building Lingotto, an investment-management arm.

records.legacy: The family's money sits in a chain: family members hold shares in Giovanni Agnelli B.V. (Netherlands), which holds about 55% of Exor N.V.; Exor in turn holds the largest stakes in Ferrari, Stellantis, Philips, CNH, Juventus and The Economist Group, and owns the asset manager Lingotto.

legacyDetail.t: Giovanni Agnelli B.V. at the top.
legacyDetail.d: Its 2025 accounts show a stable 54.9% stake in Exor and net equity of about €1.24bn after debt was almost eliminated; the Dicembre partnership (John Elkann's branch) holds about 41% of it and the Maria Sole Agnelli branch about 11% (Calcio e Finanza).
At end-2025 Exor reported NAV of €33.2bn: companies €29.2bn, Lingotto €4.2bn, other holdings €2.3bn and cash €1.4bn.

wealth.publishedNote: Forbes lists John Elkann alone; it does not publish a figure for the wider Agnelli family, whose members share Giovanni Agnelli B.V.

grossAssets.text: Exor N.V.: gross asset value €37.1bn and NAV €33.2bn at 31 December 2025 (Exor FY2025 results). Giovanni Agnelli B.V. owns 54.9% of Exor; its own net equity was about €1.24bn at book value in 2025 (it carries Exor at cost, not market value).

records.name: Quandt family (BMW, Altana)
records.scaleNote: Forbes put Stefan Quandt at $23.1bn and Susanne Klatten at $24bn in November 2026; together they held about half of BMW's ordinary shares at end-2025.
records.origins: The Quandts were textile manufacturers in Pritzwalk, Brandenburg. Günther Quandt (1881–1954) used the uniform business to buy into industry after 1918: the battery maker AFA (later Varta) and, in the 1920s–30s, the arms and munitions maker Deutsche Waffen- und Munitionsfabriken.
records.role_summary: Günther Quandt built a conglomerate of batteries, arms and metals that supplied the German war economy; the family-commissioned 2011 study found his firms used tens of thousands of forced labourers. After 1945 the family kept much of its industrial holdings. In 1959 his son Herbert Quandt bought into and rescued a struggling BMW, building the stake that his widow Johanna and children Stefan Quandt and Susanne Klatten still hold.

roleDetail.d: Günther Quandt expanded from the family textile business into AFA batteries and arms manufacturer DWM, becoming one of Germany's leading industrialists by the 1930s.

The study commissioned by the family from historian Joachim Scholtyseck (2011) concluded that Günther and Herbert Quandt were deeply involved in forced labour; press reports put the number of forced labourers in Quandt plants at about 50,000.

After the 2007 TV documentary 'Das Schweigen der Quandts', the family commissioned the study and stated that the years 1933–1945 'have not been sufficiently accounted for'. BMW itself was not implicated.
Herbert Quandt resisted a takeover of BMW by Daimler-Benz in 1959 and raised his stake, eventually to nearly half the company; it is the core of the family fortune today.
Susanne Klatten is sole owner of Altana (specialty chemicals) and holds stakes in Nordex and other firms; Stefan Quandt's AQTON SE and Delton hold Entrust, Solarwatt, Heel and Logwin.

records.legacy: BMW's ordinary shares are the core: at end-December 2025 BMW reported Stefan Quandt at 27.7% and Susanne Klatten at 22.5% of ordinary shares (25.3% and 20.5% by mid-2026 after a share-base change). Each sibling runs a single-family office: AQTON SE (Quandt) and SKion GmbH (Klatten).

legacyDetail.d: AQTON SE (Stefan Quandt) holds Entrust, Solarwatt and Scope; SKion GmbH (Susanne Klatten) holds Altana, Nordex and SKion Water; her BMW shares are held separately.
The heirs of Günther's other son Harald Quandt run a separate investment house, Harald Quandt Holding, in Bad Homburg.

wealth.publishedNote: Manager Magazin ranked Klatten and Quandt fourth in its 2026 list (down €2.8bn on 2025). Forbes lists the siblings individually.

grossAssets.text: BMW is listed; Forbes puts Stefan Quandt's stake at nearly 24% and Susanne Klatten's at about 19% of the company, and on ordinary (voting) shares alone the siblings hold close to half (reported splits vary between data providers). Altana is privately held and reports sales above $2.5bn (Forbes).

controlled.text: With roughly half of BMW's voting ordinary shares and seats on its supervisory board (Stefan Quandt is deputy chair), the siblings have decisive influence over a carmaker with more than €140bn of annual revenue.

opaque.text: The holdings are mostly in German entities with public filings (BMW voting notifications; AQTON, SKion and Altana accounts). No offshore structure was found in ICIJ data.

records.name: Porsche–Piëch family (Porsche SE, Volkswagen)
records.scaleNote: Manager Magazin put the Porsche family at €15.5bn in 2025 (4th in Baden-Württemberg); their Porsche SE holds 53.3% of Volkswagen's votes.
records.origins: Ferdinand Porsche (1875–1951), a Bohemian-born engineer, opened a design office in Stuttgart in 1931 with his son-in-law Anton Piëch and the investor Adolf Rosenberger. The office designed the Volkswagen 'KdF-Wagen' for the Nazi regime from 1934.
records.role_summary: The office earned royalties and contracts from the Volkswagen project and wartime military designs; a Porsche-commissioned study by historian Wolfram Pyta found Porsche KG employed more than 400 forced labourers. After 1948 the family built Porsche sports cars in Stuttgart and the Volkswagen import business in Austria (Porsche Holding Salzburg). A failed bid to take over VW in 2008–09 ended with VW absorbing Porsche AG, but the families' holding company, Porsche SE, emerged as VW's controlling shareholder.

roleDetail.d: Ferdinand Porsche's office designed the Volkswagen for the Nazi state from 1934, earning fees that gave the business its base.
Co-founder Adolf Rosenberger, who was Jewish, left in 1935 and sold his stake to Porsche and Piëch under 'Aryanisation' pressure; Porsche's own study has been criticised for understating this.
The Pyta study published by Porsche says Porsche KG employed more than 400 forced labourers, treated more leniently than at the VW plant; Der Spiegel had earlier put the figure at about 300.
The Porsche line ran Porsche in Stuttgart; the Piëch line ran Porsche Holding in Salzburg, Europe's large car dealership, sold to VW in 2011.
Porsche SE built up a VW stake with options and debt; the plan collapsed in the financial crisis, Porsche AG's car business was folded into VW, and Porsche SE kept a majority of VW's voting shares.

records.legacy: The families' wealth is concentrated in Porsche Automobil Holding SE (Stuttgart), whose ordinary (voting) shares are held exclusively by Porsche and Piëch family members. Porsche SE owns 53.3% of VW's ordinary shares (31.9% of capital) and 25% plus one share of Porsche AG's ordinary shares (12.5% of capital).

legacyDetail.d: Porsche SE has 153.1m voting ordinary shares (all family) and 153.1m listed non-voting preference shares; VW likewise has voting and non-voting classes.
Porsche SE wrote down its VW stake by €19.9bn and its Porsche AG stake by €3.4bn in early 2025 as car-sector valuations fell.

wealth.publishedNote: Forbes lists several family members individually; older Forbes family estimates (2001–02) were about $7bn. The Piëch branch is reported separately by Austrian media.

grossAssets.text: Porsche SE holds 53.3% of VW ordinary shares and 31.9% of subscribed capital, plus 12.5% of Porsche AG's capital; after €23bn of write-downs in early 2025 its holdings are carried well below their earlier book values.

records.name: Krupp family (Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach)
records.scaleNote: The Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation, which inherited the fortune, holds 20.93% of thyssenkrupp, the group's largest shareholder (2025).
records.lifespan: 1811–1967 as a family firm; foundation since 1967
aliases: Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach-Stiftung
records.origins: Friedrich Krupp founded a cast-steel works in Essen in 1811. His son Alfred Krupp (1812–1887) turned it into a major producer of railway steel and then cannon, earning the name 'Cannon King'.
records.role_summary: Krupp grew rich on seamless railway wheels and, above all, artillery and armour plate sold to Prussia, the German Empire and many foreign states. In the Nazi period the firm was a leading arms producer; at Nuremberg in 1948 Alfried Krupp was convicted of plunder and of using forced labour, sentenced to twelve years and forfeiture of his assets. He was released in 1951 and his property was restored; on his death in 1967 the fortune passed to a foundation, not to his heir.

roleDetail.d: Alfred Krupp expanded the Essen works from railway materials into breech-loading steel artillery from the 1850s–60s, selling to Prussia and foreign armies.
Under Friedrich Alfred Krupp and then Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach (who married the heiress Bertha), the firm became Germany's largest arms maker in both world wars.
A US military tribunal convicted Alfried Krupp of plunder in occupied territories and using forced labour and sentenced him to twelve years and forfeiture of his property.
US High Commissioner John McCloy commuted the sentence to time served in January 1951 and restored his property; Krupp resumed control of the firm in 1953.
Alfried's son Arndt renounced his inheritance in exchange for an annuity; the foundation became sole owner in 1968 and the firm became a joint-stock company.

records.legacy: The Krupp fortune today is held by the Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation in Essen, whose main asset is a 20.93% stake in thyssenkrupp AG (formed by the 1999 Krupp–Thyssen merger); dividends fund its charitable work. Villa Hügel is owned by the foundation.

legacyDetail.d: thyssenkrupp's own shareholder page shows the foundation at about 21% of the votes, with the free float at about 79%.
Because a spin-off of the steel unit needs 75% of the capital represented at the AGM, the foundation's stake gives it weight over thyssenkrupp's break-up plans.

grossAssets.text: The foundation's 20.93% thyssenkrupp stake is its principal asset; its market value moves with thyssenkrupp's share price (low single-digit € billions in 2025).

controlled.text: Largest shareholder of thyssenkrupp, a group with about €35bn of sales; it nominates supervisory-board members and is pivotal in votes on the steel spin-off.

records.name: Thyssen family (incl. Thyssen-Bornemisza)
records.scaleNote: No current rich-list figure; the Thyssen-Bornemisza collection was bought by the Spanish state for about $350m in 1993 (Sotheby's).
records.origins: August Thyssen (1842–1926), born in Eschweiler, founded a strip-iron rolling mill in Styrum near Mülheim in 1871 and built the Gewerkschaft Deutscher Kaiser steel and coal complex at Hamborn.
records.role_summary: August Thyssen built one of the Ruhr's largest vertically integrated coal and steel groups. His son Fritz chaired the 1926 steel trust Vereinigte Stahlwerke and was an early financial backer of Hitler before breaking with the regime in 1939, when his German assets were confiscated. His other son Heinrich moved to the Netherlands and Hungary (taking the name Thyssen-Bornemisza), keeping assets abroad through the Rotterdam Bank voor Handel en Scheepvaart, which became the base of the TBG group and one of Europe's great private art collections.

roleDetail.d: August Thyssen integrated mines, blast furnaces and rolling mills at Hamborn, becoming one of Germany's leading industrialists before 1914.
Fritz Thyssen became chair of the supervisory board of Vereinigte Stahlwerke, the steel trust formed in 1926, as representative of its biggest private shareholder (26%).

Fritz Thyssen supported Hitler early and joined the Nazi party in 1931, then broke with the regime over the war in 1939; his German fortune was confiscated. The book 'I Paid Hitler' (1941) was ghost-written and historians treat it as unreliable.

The Bank voor Handel en Scheepvaart in Rotterdam (founded by the family around 1916–18) handled the family's assets abroad; its US affiliate Union Banking Corporation was seized by the US government in 1942.
Hans Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza sold 775 works to the Spanish state in 1993 for about $350m, forming the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.

records.legacy: The Thyssen steel business merged with Krupp in 1999 to form thyssenkrupp; the family holds no significant stake today. The Fritz Thyssen Stiftung (founded 1959 by Fritz's widow and daughter) funds research. The Thyssen-Bornemisza line's wealth sits in private holdings and art, including Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza's collection on loan to Spain.

legacyDetail.d: The Spanish state owns the 1993 collection; Carmen Cervera's separate collection has been on loan, with long-running negotiations over its future.

ICIJ reported in 2013 that Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza bought art at auction through a Cook Islands company; her lawyer said tax havens gave 'maximum flexibility' in moving art. Being listed in ICIJ data does not imply wrongdoing.

wealth.publishedNote: No current Forbes, Bloomberg or Manager Magazin figure for the Thyssen or Thyssen-Bornemisza families was found.

grossAssets.text: Not public. The family's industrial stake was diluted in the 1999 Krupp merger; the main documented values are the art sales ($350m in 1993).

controlled.text: The Fritz Thyssen Stiftung is a research foundation, not a family vehicle; the museum is state-owned. No documented control over listed companies today.

opaque.text: ICIJ's 2013 Offshore Leaks reporting named Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza and her son Borja as holding art through offshore companies, and said Hans Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza had used structures such as a Bermuda trust company to manage money and art; her lawyer said tax havens offered 'maximum flexibility' in moving paintings. In 2016 EFE reported that family members also appear in the Panama Papers; the family's lawyer confirmed ownership of an offshore company and said the Spanish tax authorities had full knowledge of it. Being listed in ICIJ data does not imply wrongdoing.

records.scaleNote: Wendel-Participations SE, owned by about 1,400 family members and entities, holds 41.1% of Wendel SE, a listed investor whose fully diluted NAV was €164.2 per share at end-2025.
aliases: Les Petits-Fils de François de Wendel
records.origins: Jean-Martin Wendel bought the forges of Hayange in Lorraine in 1704, starting nearly three centuries of family iron- and steelmaking in the Moselle valley.
records.role_summary: The Wendels built one of France's largest iron and steel groups in Lorraine, supplying rails, plate and armaments; the family straddled the French–German border after the 1871 annexation of Moselle. When the steel crisis led to nationalisation in 1978, the family converted its holding into an investment company (later Wendel), which bought and sold stakes in companies such as Legrand, Bureau Veritas and Saint-Gobain.

roleDetail.d: Jean-Martin Wendel acquired the Hayange ironworks; his descendants expanded across Lorraine (Hayange, Moyeuvre, Joeuf).
By the 19th and 20th centuries de Wendel was among France's leading steelmakers, and François de Wendel sat in parliament as a deputy for Moselle.
The steel crisis and state takeover of the industry ended the family's industrial chapter; the family regrouped its capital in an investment holding.

Wendel bought and relisted Legrand (2002), floated Bureau Veritas in 2007 while keeping a majority, and made a leveraged 2007 investment in Saint-Gobain; in December 2010 the AMF's sanctions committee fined Wendel and Jean-Bernard Lafonta, then chairman of its management board, €1.5m each for failing to inform the market of the derivative contracts used to prepare the Saint-Gobain stake; Wendel disputed the finding and appealed.

records.legacy: The family's capital sits in Wendel-Participations SE, which holds 41.1% of Wendel SE. Wendel holds stakes in Bureau Veritas, IHS Towers, Scalian, Globeducate, ACAMS and others, and since 2024–25 owns the third-party asset managers IK Partners and Monroe Capital (Wendel Investment Managers).

legacyDetail.d: Wendel-Participations' statutes require approval of share transfers to keep the holding in family hands; it gathers about 1,400 family members and entities.
Wendel's 2025 results reported about €160m of pro-forma fee-related earnings from IK Partners and Monroe Capital.

records.name: Schneider family (Schneider et Cie, Le Creusot)
records.scaleNote: At its peak Schneider et Cie was one of Europe's leading arms makers (by 1871, per Schneider Electric); the family lost control to the Empain group in the 1960s and has no major fortune today.
records.origins: The brothers Adolphe and Eugène Schneider, from Lorraine, bought the iron-ore mines and forges of Le Creusot in 1836 with backing from Paris bankers, including the Seillière family.
records.role_summary: The Schneiders turned Le Creusot into France's great heavy-engineering town: rails, the first French locomotives, steamships, steel and, from the 1870s, artillery and armour plate sold to France and foreign states. Eugène Schneider was also a minister and president of the Corps législatif. After World War II the group dropped arms; after Charles Schneider died in 1960 the Belgian Empain group took control (1963) and merged in 1969, the root of today's Schneider Electric.

roleDetail.d: Adolphe and Eugène Schneider acquired the mines and forges and built a business in steel, railways, armaments and shipbuilding.
By 1871 Schneider et Cie had become one of Europe's main arms manufacturers, a rival of Krupp in guns and armour plate.
The family built housing, schools and churches at Le Creusot, a classic 19th-century company town.
After Charles Schneider's death in 1960 the Empain group took control (1963) and merged in 1969 into Empain-Schneider, renamed Schneider SA (1980) and Schneider Electric (1999).

records.legacy: No Schneider family holding of significance survives; the company's heir is Schneider Electric, a widely held listed group with no controlling family. The family's château at Le Creusot is now a museum site owned by the town.

legacyDetail.d: Schneider Electric dropped arms after 1945 and became an electrical-equipment group; its shares are widely held.

records.role_summary: The family grew from steel tools into bicycles and, under Armand Peugeot in the 1890s, cars. PSA (Peugeot, then Citroën from 1976) made the family France's leading car dynasty.
